title: Electromagnetic induction
headline: Induction: change in flux, not merely the presence of a magnet
summary: Changing flux, Lenz law, induced fields, transformers, and RL circuits.

sections.title: Magnetic flux and all three routes to a changing flux
sections.search:
## Induction: change in flux, not merely the presence of a magnet

An induced emf can exist without a closed conducting circuit. A closed path is required for the ordinary induced current examples. A stationary loop in a time-varying magnetic field can have emf even when no wire moves. Conversely, motion that leaves the relevant flux unchanged need not produce a net loop emf.

Magnetic flux and all three routes to a changing flux

$$\Phi_B=\int\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A,\quad \Phi_B=BA\cos\theta\ \text{for uniform }B.$$

The angle is between B and the AREA NORMAL. If a problem gives the angle to the plane, use the complementary angle. One weber is one $T \cdot m^{2}$. A field perpendicular to the plane produces maximum flux magnitude; a field parallel to the plane produces zero flux.

If B occupies only an overlap area, integrate over that region. Primary p. 10 has flux $BA_{2}$, not $BA_{1}$, when the field is confined to the smaller perpendicular overlap area $A_{2}$. Treat “zero outside the field region” explicitly.

**Worked example — primary p. 11.** A $0.100\,\mathrm{m}$ square loop in $1.25\,\mathrm{T}$ has $A = 0.0100\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$. Maximum magnitude: $0.0125\,\mathrm{Wb}$; minimum magnitude: $0$. Signed flux can range from −0.0125 to $+ 0.0125\,\mathrm{Wb}$ depending on the chosen normal.

sections.title: Faraday's law and the full product derivative
sections.search:
Faraday's law and the full product derivative

Faraday's law is a fundamental induction law in this course. For N turns linking the same flux, $\mathcal{E} = - \frac{N d\Phi B}{dt}$. For nonidentical linked fluxes, sum the flux linkages instead of assuming $N\Phi$. The finite average magnitude is $\frac{N \left| \Delta \Phi \right|}{\Delta t}$; it equals the instantaneous value only for a constant rate during the interval.

$$\mathcal E=-N\left(A\cos\theta\frac{dB}{dt}+B\cos\theta\frac{dA}{dt}-BA\sin\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right).$$

This product-rule expression covers changing field strength, changing area, changing orientation, and simultaneous changes. Set only the quantities explicitly held constant to zero.

**Worked example — primary p. 18.** $N = 200$; square side: $0.180\,\mathrm{m}$; $R = 2.0 \Omega$; $\Delta B = 0.500\,\mathrm{T}$ in $0.80\,\mathrm{s}$, with perpendicular field. $A = 0.0324\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$. $\left| \mathcal{E} \right| = \frac{200 \left( 0.0324 \right) \left( 0.500 \right)}{0.80} = 4.05\,\mathrm{V}$. Current magnitude: $\frac{4.05}{2.0} = 2.025\,\mathrm{A}$. The source's $4.1\,\mathrm{V}$ is rounded.

sections.title: Lenz's law with four direction cases
sections.search:
Lenz's law with four direction cases

Choose the external field direction, then determine whether its flux increases or decreases. The induced field OPPOSES THE CHANGE, not necessarily the external field. Use the right-hand grip rule to convert the required induced field into conventional current.

| External flux seen by the observer | Required induced field | Induced current as seen by that observer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Into page, increasing | Out of page | Counterclockwise |
| Into page, decreasing | Into page | Clockwise |
| Out of page, increasing | Into page | Clockwise |
| Out of page, decreasing | Out of page | Counterclockwise |

Primary p. 28 prints a decreasing inward-field example with the wrong outward induced field. For its stated inward and decreasing flux, the correction is inward induced field and clockwise current. Always check the actual loop position and arrow before applying a memorized wire-direction answer.

sections.title: Motional emf from two derivations
sections.search:
Motional emf from two derivations

**Flux derivation.** A rod of length ℓ slides distance dx in a perpendicular uniform B. The loop's area change is $dA = \ell dx$, so $\left| \mathcal{E} \right| = B \ell \left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right) = B \ell v$.

**Charge-force derivation.** Charges in an open moving rod redistribute until qE balances the magnetic qvB. Thus $E = vB$, and voltage magnitude $E \ell = B \ell v$. The general expression is $\int \left( v \times B \right) \cdot dl$; the product Bℓv needs the stated perpendicular geometry.

For a sliding rod in a closed resistance R: $I = \frac{B \ell v}{R}$. Magnetic drag magnitude is $F = I \ell B = \frac{B^{2} \ell^{2} v}{R}$. Required mechanical power at constant speed is $Fv = I^{2} R$, which verifies energy conservation.

**Worked example — primary p. 35.** Speed $\frac{1000\,\mathrm{km}}{h} = 277.778\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$. A $70\,\mathrm{m}$ wingspan moving perpendicular to a nearly vertical $5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ field develops about $0.9722\,\mathrm{V}$ between tips. Which tip is positive depends on the velocity and field vector directions.

sections.title: Generators, microphones, transformers, and eddy currents
sections.search:
Generators, microphones, transformers, and eddy currents

For a rigid rotating N-turn coil, $\Phi = BA\cos \left( \omega t + \phi \right)$. Differentiate to derive $\mathcal{E} \left( t \right) = NBA\omega \sin \left( \omega t + \phi \right)$, with peak $NBA\omega$. A GENERATOR converts mechanical input into electrical output. Primary p. 14 reverses that conversion in its wording; it describes motor action instead. A moving-coil microphone converts mechanical vibration into an electrical signal.

An ideal transformer links both windings to the same changing core flux. Dividing their Faraday equations gives $\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$. With ideal power conservation, $V_{p} I_{p} = V_{s} I_{s}$ and $\frac{I_{s}}{I_{p}} = \frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}$. These are compatible AC magnitudes, usually rms values. A transformer does not directly convert AC into DC; a rectifier and other power-supply stages are required.

**Worked example — primary p. 19.** Ideal $120\,\mathrm{V}$ to $9\,\mathrm{V}$ AC, $N_{s} = 30$, $I_{s} = 0.400\,\mathrm{A}$ gives $N_{p} = 400$ turns, output power: $3.6\,\mathrm{W}$, and input current: $0.030\,\mathrm{A}$. The slide's description of $9\,\mathrm{V}$ DC includes an implicit rectifier; the transformer equations alone address the AC stage.

Eddy currents circulate in bulk conductors. Their opposing magnetic effects can slow moving metal. Energy becomes heat. A changing current in one coil can induce emf in a nearby coil even without a conducting connection between them.

sections.title: Mutual/self-inductance and stored magnetic energy
sections.search:
Mutual/self-inductance and stored magnetic energy

Define mutual inductance through $\mathcal{E}_{2} = - \frac{M dI_{1}}{dt}$. For a linear coil, flux linkage $N\Phi = LI$, giving $\mathcal{E} _{\mathrm{self}} = - \frac{L dI}{dt}$. L and M have units henry: $\frac{V \cdot s}{A} = \Omega \cdot s$. Constant permeability and fixed geometry are part of the simple constant-L model.

For an ideal long solenoid, $B = \frac{\mu NI}{\ell}$. Flux per turn is BA. Therefore $L = \frac{N\Phi}{I} = \frac{\mathrm{\mu N}^{2} A}{\ell}$. Derive stored energy by $P = LI \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)$ and integrate: $U = \int_{0} ᴵ Li di = \frac{LI^{2}}{2}$. Inductors resist a CHANGE in current; they do not simply “oppose current” in every situation.

Substitute $L = \frac{\mathrm{\mu N}^{2} A}{\ell}$ into $U = \frac{LI^{2}}{2}$ and replace $\frac{NI}{\ell}$ with $\frac{B}{\mu}$. This gives $U = \frac{B^{2} A \ell}{\left( 2 \mu \right)}$. Divide by the solenoid's internal field volume Aℓ to get magnetic energy density $u_{B} = \frac{B^{2}}{\left( 2 \mu \right)}$. Compare the electric result $u_{E} = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2}}{2}$. Both formulas assume the specified linear material model.

sections.title: RL growth, decay, and arbitrary initial current
sections.search:
RL growth, decay, and arbitrary initial current

KVL for an ideal L in series with total R gives $\mathcal{E} = L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right) + RI$. Separate and integrate with $I \left( 0 \right) = 0$:

$$I(t)=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}(1-e^{-tR/L}),\quad \tau_{RL}=L/R.$$

After removing the source while retaining a closed R–L path, $I = I_{0} \exp \left( - \frac{t R}{L} \right)$. More generally $I(t)=I_f+(I_0-I_f)e^{-t/\tau}$. Inductor current is continuous in this ideal finite-voltage model. At DC steady state, an ideal inductor has zero voltage; real winding resistance remains.

For fraction f of final growth, $t = - \left( \frac{L}{R} \right) \ln \left( 1 - f \right)$. For remaining decay fraction f, $t = - \left( \frac{L}{R} \right) \ln f$. RC increases its time constant with R; RL decreases its time constant with R. Do not interchange them.

**Worked example — primary p. 44.** $L = 87.5\,\mathrm{mH} = 0.0875\,\mathrm{H}$ and $R = 0.250 \Omega$. $\tau = 0.350\,\mathrm{s}$. Growth reaches $1 - e^{-1} = 63.212$% at $0.350\,\mathrm{s}$. Exactly 63% requires $- 0.350 \ln \left( 0.37 \right) \approx 0.348\,\mathrm{s}$. The printed “63%” convention is a rounding approximation.

**Show the RL integration.** Rearrange the loop equation to $\frac{dI}{\left( \mathcal{E} - RI \right)} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrate using $I \left( 0 \right) = 0$. The left side contributes $- \frac{\ln \left[ \frac{\left( \mathcal{E} - RI \right)}{\mathcal{E}} \right]}{R}$. Therefore:

$$-\ln\left(1-\frac{RI}{\mathcal E}\right)=\frac{Rt}{L}\Rightarrow I=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}(1-e^{-Rt/L}).$$

For $\mathcal{E} = 12\,\mathrm{V}$, $R = 6 \Omega$, and $L = 3\,\mathrm{H}$, $\tau = 0.5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $I_{\mathrm{final}} = 2\,\mathrm{A}$. At one time constant, $I \approx 1.26424\,\mathrm{A}$. The resistor drop is $7.58545\,\mathrm{V}$; the inductor drop is $\mathcal{E} e^{-1} \approx 4.41455\,\mathrm{V}$. Their sum remains $12\,\mathrm{V}$. Initial current is zero, while the initial inductor drop is the full $12\,\mathrm{V}$. At long times, the ideal inductor drop tends to zero and stored energy tends to $\tfrac{1}{2} \left( 3 \right) \left( 2^{2} \right) = 6\,\mathrm{J}$.

**Switching check.** A source-free decay needs a closed path. Opening the only path does not make a real inductor's current disappear without consequence. Its induced voltage can become large and cause a spark or flow through a protection component. The simple exponential requires a valid R–L discharge path.

sections.title: Flux signs, partial overlap, and the induction experiment
sections.search:
Flux signs, partial overlap, and the induction experiment

**Starting and stopping the primary-coil current — primary pp. 5–7.** A steady primary current produces a steady field. A stationary secondary loop then has no transformer emf from that constant flux. Starting or stopping the primary current changes the shared flux and produces a secondary emf. The two coils need no conducting connection for this energy transfer.

**Flux sign convention.** Choose a surface normal first. A field component along that normal gives positive flux; the opposite component gives negative flux. Couple the positive loop direction to the normal by the right-hand grip rule. The Faraday minus sign then has a precise directional meaning.

:::example Partial magnetic-field overlap
**Source:** Primary p. 10. The loop encloses area $A_{1}$, but a perpendicular field exists only over a smaller enclosed area $A_{2}$.

1. Split the flux integral into the field region and the zero-field region.
2. Calculate $\Phi = BA_{2} + 0 \left( A_{1} - A_{2} \right) = BA_{2}$ for the aligned positive normal.
3. Reverse the surface normal to reverse the signed flux.

**Check.** $BA_{1}$ would incorrectly assign a nonzero field to the whole loop interior. The relevant area is the area where field actually passes through the chosen surface.
:::

:::example Maximum and minimum flux through the square loop
**Source:** Primary p. 11. **Given:** Side $10.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.100\,\mathrm{m}$ and $B = 1.25\,\mathrm{T}$.

1. Find $A = \left( 0.100 \right)^{2} = 0.0100\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$.
2. Use $\Phi = BA\cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is measured from the area normal.
3. Find the maximum magnitude at $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ or 180°: $|\Phi|_{\max}=0.0125\,\mathrm{Wb}$.
4. Find zero flux at $\theta = 90^{\circ}$.

**Wording check.** The minimum magnitude is zero. The minimum signed flux over all orientations is $- 0.0125\,\mathrm{Wb}$. State which meaning of “minimum” you use.
:::

sections.title: Full Faraday and transformer solutions
sections.search:
Full Faraday and transformer solutions

:::derivation The AC generator waveform and rotation units
**Source starting point:** Primary p. 14. Let a rigid N-turn coil of area A rotate at constant angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform field. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the area normal and B.

1. Write $\theta \left( t \right) = \omega t + \phi$, with angles in radians.
2. Write the flux per turn as $\Phi = BA\cos \left( \omega t + \phi \right)$.
3. Differentiate the cosine: $\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = - BA\omega \sin \left( \omega t + \phi \right)$.
4. Apply Faraday's minus sign and multiply by N.

$$\mathcal E(t)=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi),
\qquad \mathcal E_{peak}=NBA\omega,
\qquad \omega=2\pi f.$$

At maximum flux, the instantaneous flux slope and emf are zero. When the flux passes through zero during this rotation, the emf magnitude reaches its peak. Mechanical rotation supplies the electrical output energy. Do not substitute rotation frequency f in hertz directly for $\omega$ in radians per second.
:::

:::example The 200-turn square coil: emf and current
**Source:** Primary p. 18. **Given:** $N = 200$, side: $0.180\,\mathrm{m}$, $R_{\mathrm{total}} = 2.0 \Omega$, and perpendicular B rising from 0 to $0.500\,\mathrm{T}$ in $0.80\,\mathrm{s}$.

1. Find $A = 0.180^{2} = 0.0324\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$ for one turn.
2. Find the rate $\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.500}{0.80} = 0.625\,\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{s}}$.
3. Use $\left| \mathcal{E} \right| = NA \left| \frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} \right| = 200 \left( 0.0324 \right) \left( 0.625 \right) = 4.05\,\mathrm{V}$.
4. Find the induced-current magnitude $I = \frac{\left| \mathcal{E} \right|}{R_{\mathrm{total}}} = \frac{4.05}{2.0} = 2.025\,\mathrm{A}$.
5. Find the direction separately with Lenz's law, using the actual external field direction.

**Check.** The coil's 2.0 Ω is already its total resistance. Do not multiply that resistance by the number of turns again.
:::

:::derivation Transformer turns and current ratios
**Sources:** Primary pp. 16–19. Assume ideal coupling, a common changing core flux per turn, and negligible losses.

1. Write the induced-voltage magnitudes $V_{p} = N_{p} \left| \frac{d\Phi}{dt} \right|$ and $V_{s} = N_{s} \left| \frac{d\Phi}{dt} \right|$.
2. Divide to cancel the common flux-change rate.
3. Use ideal average-power conservation for matching AC quantities.

$$\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{N_s}{N_p},\qquad
V_pI_p=V_sI_s,\qquad
\frac{I_s}{I_p}=\frac{N_p}{N_s}.$$

A step-up transformer increases voltage and decreases current for the same ideal transferred power. A step-down transformer does the reverse. Current does not travel across the insulation from one winding into the other. The changing magnetic field couples the circuits.
:::

:::example Radio power supply: identify the ideal AC stage
**Source:** Primary p. 19. Use $V_{p} = 120\,\mathrm{V}$ AC, $V_{s} = 9.0\,\mathrm{V}$ AC for the transformer calculation, $N_{s} = 30$, and $I_{s} = 0.400\,\mathrm{A}$.

1. Rearrange the turns ratio: $N_{p} = \frac{N_{s} V_{p}}{V_{s}} = \frac{30 \left( 120 \right)}{9.0} = 400$ turns.
2. Find secondary power: $P_{s} = V_{s} I_{s} = 9.0 \left( 0.400 \right) = 3.6\,\mathrm{W}$.
3. Use ideal input power $P_{p} = 3.6\,\mathrm{W}$.
4. Find $I_{p} = \frac{P_{p}}{V_{p}} = \frac{3.6}{120} = 0.030\,\mathrm{A}$.

**Source correction.** The question describes a $9\,\mathrm{V}$ DC radio supply. A transformer alone supplies AC. Rectification and filtering are additional stages; the ideal turns-ratio calculation describes the AC transformer stage.
:::

For each drawing, first derive the external field from the straight wire's current and the loop's position. The same upward wire current has opposite field directions on opposite sides of the wire. Do not transfer an inward-field answer to a loop drawn on the other side.

:::example The moving bar: polarity, current, drag, and power
**Source geometry:** Primary pp. 31–33. The following numerical values form a labeled extension: $B = 0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ out of the page, vertical bar length $\ell = 0.20\,\mathrm{m}$, rightward speed $v = 3.0\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$, and loop resistance $R = 2.0 \Omega$.

1. Find $v \times B$: right × out points down. Positive charges collect toward the bar's lower end.
2. Calculate the emf magnitude: $\left| \mathcal{E} \right| = B \ell v = 0.50 \left( 0.20 \right) \left( 3.0 \right) = 0.300\,\mathrm{V}$.
3. Calculate $I = \frac{\left| \mathcal{E} \right|}{R} = 0.150\,\mathrm{A}$. The bar carries current downward, so the loop current is clockwise.
4. Calculate the magnetic force on the bar: $F_{\mathrm{mag}} = I \ell B = 0.0150\,\mathrm{N}$ left.
5. Apply $0.0150\,\mathrm{N}$ right to maintain the constant speed.
6. Calculate mechanical input power: $Fv = 0.0450\,\mathrm{W}$.
7. Check resistive heating: $I^{2} R = 0.150^{2} \left( 2.0 \right) = 0.0450\,\mathrm{W}$.

**Check.** Increasing outward flux induces an inward field, consistent with clockwise current. The force opposes the motion, not the existence of the bar itself.
:::

:::example Airplane wing-tip potential difference
**Source:** Primary p. 35. **Given:** Speed $\frac{1000\,\mathrm{km}}{h}$, vertical $B = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$, and wingspan $70\,\mathrm{m}$. Use the stated perpendicular geometry.

1. Convert speed: $v = \frac{1000 \left( 1000 \right)}{3600} = 277.778\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$.
2. Calculate $\left| \Delta V \right| = B \ell v = \left( 5.0 \times 10^{-5} \right) \left( 70 \right) \left( 277.778 \right) = 0.972222\,\mathrm{V}$.
3. Determine which wing tip is positive with $v \times B$ for positive charge carriers.

**Geometry check.** The numerical statement gives a magnitude but does not fully identify a compass heading and field sign. Do not invent a left-wing or right-wing polarity without those directions.

sections.title: The missing distinction: induced electric fields are not electrostatic fields
sections.search:
The missing distinction: induced electric fields are not electrostatic fields

**Sources:** Primary objectives on p. 23 and discussion on p. 34. A changing magnetic flux creates a circulating electric field. It can act on a charge initially at rest. A conducting wire is not required for the electric field to exist.

For electrostatics, a single-valued scalar potential gives $E = - \nabla V$ and $\oint E \cdot dl = 0$. In induction, the closed-loop integral can be nonzero:

$$\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.$$

The $E = vB$ inside a moving open rod instead describes charge separation that balances $qv \times B$ in that rod. It is not a universal formula for the circulating field around every changing magnetic field.

:::derivation Induced field inside and outside a circular changing-field region
This labeled extension develops the source objective. Let uniform B(t) point along +z inside radius a and be zero outside. Choose counterclockwise circulation as positive.

1. By cylindrical symmetry, E is tangent to a centered circle and has constant magnitude along it.
2. The circulation is $E\phi \left( 2 \pi r \right)$.
3. For $r \le a$, the enclosed magnetic flux is $\pi r^{2} B$.
4. For $r \ge a$, the enclosed magnetic flux is $\pi a^{2} B$.
5. Apply Faraday's law and solve each region separately.

$$E_\phi(r)=\begin{cases}
-\dfrac r2\dfrac{dB}{dt},&r\le a,\\[6pt]
-\dfrac{a^2}{2r}\dfrac{dB}{dt},&r\ge a.
\end{cases}$$

**Checks.** Both expressions agree at $r = a$. E tends to zero at the center. Outside, E can remain nonzero even where the local magnetic field is zero, because the loop encloses changing flux. For increasing +z flux, $E\phi$ is negative, so the circulation is clockwise.
:::

sections.title: Mutual inductance, self-inductance, and complete RL decay
sections.search:
Mutual inductance, self-inductance, and complete RL decay

:::derivation Derive self-inductance from flux linkage
**Sources:** Primary pp. 37–41. For a linear coil, the total linkage is $\Lambda = N\Phi = LI$. If L is constant, differentiation gives $\frac{d \Lambda}{dt} = L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)$. Faraday's law therefore gives $\mathcal{E} _{\mathrm{self}} = - L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)$.

For a long solenoid, substitute $B = \frac{\mu NI}{\ell}$ into $\Phi = BA$:

$$L=\frac{N\Phi}{I}
=\frac{N(\mu NI/\ell)A}{I}
=\frac{\mu N^2A}{\ell}.$$

For mutual inductance, use $\Lambda_{2} = N_{2} \Phi_{21} = MI_{1}$, so $\mathcal{E}_{2} = - M \left( \frac{dI_{1}}{dt} \right)$ for constant geometry and a linear material. A steady current gives no induced emf from these constant-linkage terms.
:::

:::example Interpret a mutual- or self-induced emf measurement
**Labeled extension of primary pp. 38–39.** Let $M = 0.040\,\mathrm{H}$ and let primary current rise by $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in $0.010\,\mathrm{s}$.

1. Find the average current-change rate: $\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 200\,\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{s}}$.
2. Calculate the secondary emf magnitude: $\left| \mathcal{E}_{2} \right| = M \left| \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \right| = 8.0\,\mathrm{V}$.
3. Set its polarity with the chosen winding directions and Lenz's law.

For a self-inductor $L = 0.20\,\mathrm{H}$ whose current rises by $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in $0.050\,\mathrm{s}$, the average opposing-emf magnitude is $12\,\mathrm{V}$. The negative sign describes opposition to the current change. It does not mean the inductance is negative.
:::

:::derivation RL decay and the fraction-of-current time
**Sources:** Primary pp. 42–44. Remove the source while retaining a closed series R–L path. Choose the continuing current as positive.

1. Write the loop equation $L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right) + RI = 0$.
2. Separate $\frac{dI}{I} = - \left( \frac{R}{L} \right) dt$.
3. Integrate from $I_{0}$ at time zero to I(t).
4. Exponentiate, then isolate time for a specified remaining fraction.

$$\ln\frac{I}{I_0}=-\frac{R}{L}t
\Rightarrow I=I_0e^{-tR/L},
\qquad t=\frac LR\ln\frac{I_0}{I}.$$

The initial magnetic energy, $\tfrac{1}{2} LI_{0}^{2}$, becomes resistor heating during an ideal source-free decay. The current remains continuous through switching when the circuit supplies a finite-voltage discharge path.
:::

:::example The source's $87.5\,\mathrm{mH}$ coil
**Source:** Primary p. 44. **Given:** $L = 87.5\,\mathrm{mH} = 0.0875\,\mathrm{H}$ and total series $R = 0.250 \Omega$.

1. Calculate $\tau = \frac{L}{R} = \frac{0.0875}{0.250} = 0.350\,\mathrm{s}$.
2. For growth from zero, use $\frac{I}{I_{\mathrm{final}}} = 1 - \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\tau} \right)$.
3. Set the exact requested fraction 0.63: $0.37 = \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\tau} \right)$.
4. Calculate $t = - 0.350 \ln \left( 0.37 \right) = 0.347989\,\mathrm{s}$, about $0.348\,\mathrm{s}$.
5. If “63%” means the usual rounded one-time-constant result, $t \approx 0.350\,\mathrm{s}$. At that time the exact fraction is 63.2121%.

**Check.** The battery voltage cancels because the problem asks for a fraction of the final current. Include winding resistance in the total R.
:::

| Circuit at a constant DC source | At the start, from an unenergized state | At long times | Time constant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Series RC | $V_{C} = 0$; current starts at $\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}$ | $V_{C} \to \mathcal{E}$; current → 0 | RC |
| Series RL | $I = 0$; inductor initially has the source voltage | $I \to \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}$; ideal inductor voltage → 0 | $\frac{L}{R}$ |

Increasing R makes RC charging slower for fixed C. Increasing R makes the RL normalized transient faster for fixed L, while also lowering its final current. Compare fractions and final values separately.

Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation These worked examples apply the module concepts. Each example states its conditions, explains the model, and shows the complete working.

Worked application 1: Zero flux does not mean zero emf

A rigid loop rotates at constant angular speed in a uniform magnetic field. At one instant its magnetic flux is zero. The rotating-loop model compares instantaneous flux with induced emf when the flux is zero. 1. **Write the flux.** $$\Phi=BA\cos(\omega t)$$ 2. **Differentiate it.** $$\mathcal E=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$$ 3. **Check the zero-flux orientation.** $$\cos(\omega t)=0\ \Rightarrow\ |\sin(\omega t)|=1$$ 4. **Keep the distinction.** The field, area, or orientation can change the flux. **Result:** Yes. For sinusoidal flux, its magnitude is maximum when flux crosses zero.

Worked application 2: Lenz direction for a weakening field

A conducting loop lies in the page. A uniform external magnetic field points out of the page and decreases in magnitude. Lenz’s law determines the induced conventional-current direction, viewed from the front, as the outward field decreases. 1. **Identify the change.** Outward flux is decreasing. 2. **Oppose that change.** The induced field must point outward. 3. **Apply the loop right-hand rule.** An outward thumb gives counterclockwise curled fingers. 4. **Check the wording.** The induced field opposes the change, rather than always opposing the external field. **Result:** Counterclockwise.

Worked application 3: The same initial and final flux

The magnetic flux through a fixed N-turn coil changes and later returns to its initial value. Faraday’s law determines the time integral of the induced emf over the entire interval when the initial flux returns. 1. **Start from Faraday’s law.** $$\mathcal E=-N\,d\Phi/dt$$ 2. **Integrate with a fixed orientation.** $$\int_{t_i}^{t_f}\mathcal E\,dt=-N(\Phi_f-\Phi_i)$$ 3. **Use the equal endpoint values.** $$\Phi_f=\Phi_i\ \Rightarrow\ \int\mathcal E\,dt=0$$ 4. **Avoid an extra conclusion.** The emf can be nonzero during parts of the interval. **Result:** It is zero: $\int\mathcal E\,dt=0$.

Worked application 4: A transformer after the DC transient

A transformer primary has nonzero winding resistance. A DC source has been connected long enough for its current and core flux to become constant. Ignore leakage and saturation. The constant final core flux determines the secondary induced emf after the DC transient ends. 1. **Identify the stated steady condition.** After the transient, the current and flux are constant. 2. **Apply Faraday’s law to the secondary.** $$\mathcal E_s=-N_s\,d\Phi/dt$$ 3. **Use the zero derivative.** $$d\Phi/dt=0\ \Rightarrow\ \mathcal E_s=0$$ 4. **Separate switching from steady operation.** Connection and disconnection can produce transient secondary emf. **Result:** Zero.

Worked application 5: An inductor starts to discharge

An inductor carrying current is disconnected from its source and connected into a closed loop with a finite resistor. Inductor-current continuity determines the current immediately after switching into the closed resistor loop. 1. **Use the inductor relation.** $$V_L=L\,di/dt$$ 2. **Write the source-free loop equation.** $$L\,di/dt+Ri=0$$ 3. **Use current continuity.** $$i(t)=I_0e^{-Rt/L},\quad i(0^+)=I_0$$ 4. **Check energy transfer.** The resistor dissipates the magnetic energy initially stored in the inductor. **Result:** Current starts from its previous value and then decays continuously.

Worked application 6: Both field and area change

A 100-turn coil has a uniform perpendicular field $B(t)=(0.20+0.10t)\,\mathrm T$ and area $A(t)=(0.030-0.002t)\,\mathrm{m^2}$, with t in seconds. Choose positive flux along the field and positive emf around its right-hand-rule contour. The calculation determines the signed induced emf at $t=2.0\,\mathrm s$. 1. **Use flux per turn.** $$\Phi(t)=B(t)A(t)$$ 2. **Differentiate both changing factors.** $$\mathcal E=-N[A\,dB/dt+B\,dA/dt]$$ 3. **Evaluate the instantaneous quantities.** $$B(2)=0.40\,\mathrm T,\quad A(2)=0.026\,\mathrm{m^2}$$ 4. **Substitute both contributions.** $$\mathcal E=-100[(0.026)(0.10)+(0.40)(-0.002)]=-0.180\,\mathrm V$$ 5. **Interpret the sign.** Field growth dominates area shrinkage, so positive flux increases and the emf acts in the negative contour direction. 6. **State the result.** $$-0.18\,\mathrm V$$ **Result:** $-0.18\,\mathrm V$

Worked application 7: Emf of a rotating coil

A 100-turn coil of area 0.010 m² rotates in a uniform 0.20 T field at 50 rad/s. Its normal makes an increasing angle of 30° with the field. The calculation determines the instantaneous induced emf magnitude. 1. **Write the angle-dependent flux.** $$\Phi=BA\cos\theta$$ 2. **Differentiate using angular speed.** $$|\mathcal E|=NBA\omega|\sin\theta|$$ 3. **Substitute.** $$|\mathcal E|=(100)(0.20)(0.010)(50)\sin30^\circ=5.00\,\mathrm V$$ 4. **Check the angle.** Use the angle to the normal. The maximum occurs at a normal angle of 90°. 5. **State the result.** $$5\,\mathrm V$$ **Result:** $5\,\mathrm V$

Worked application 8: Mechanical power in a sliding rod

A 0.40 m conducting rod slides at constant 3.0 m/s on ideal rails in a uniform 0.50 T field. The rod, velocity, and field are mutually perpendicular. The closed circuit has total resistance 2.0 Ω. Ignore friction and self-inductance. The calculation determines the external mechanical power needed. 1. **Find motional emf.** $$\mathcal E=BLv=(0.50)(0.40)(3.0)=0.60\,\mathrm V$$ 2. **Find the current.** $$I=\mathcal E/R=0.60/2.0=0.30\,\mathrm A$$ 3. **Find magnetic drag and balance it.** $$F_{\mathrm{ext}}=BIL=(0.50)(0.30)(0.40)=0.060\,\mathrm N$$ 4. **Calculate mechanical power.** $$P=F_{\mathrm{ext}}v=(0.060)(3.0)=0.180\,\mathrm W$$ 5. **Check electrical heating.** $$I^2R=(0.30)^2(2.0)=0.180\,\mathrm W$$ 6. **State the result.** $$0.18\,\mathrm W$$ **Result:** $0.18\,\mathrm W$

Worked application 9: An RL circuit reaches a chosen current

A 12 V ideal source is connected to a series 6.0 Ω resistor and 3.0 H ideal inductor. The initial current is zero. The calculation determines the time when current first reaches 75% of its final value. 1. **Calculate the final current and time constant.** $$I_\infty=12/6=2.0\,\mathrm A,\quad\tau=L/R=3/6=0.50\,\mathrm s$$ 2. **Use the growth solution.** $$i/I_\infty=1-e^{-t/\tau}$$ 3. **Isolate the remaining fraction.** $$e^{-t/\tau}=1-0.75=0.25$$ 4. **Take logarithms.** $$t=-0.50\ln0.25=0.50\ln4$$ 5. **Check the time.** Reaching 75% takes more than one time constant. 6. **State the result.** $$0.693147\,\mathrm s$$ **Result:** $0.693147\,\mathrm s$

Worked application 10: Transformer input current under load

An ideal transformer receives 24 V rms at its 100-turn primary. Its 500-turn secondary supplies a 240 Ω resistor. Use sinusoidal steady operation. The calculation determines the primary rms current. 1. **Find the secondary rms voltage.** $$V_s=V_pN_s/N_p=24(500/100)=120\,\mathrm V$$ 2. **Find secondary current.** $$I_s=V_s/R=120/240=0.50\,\mathrm A$$ 3. **Use ideal power conservation.** $$V_pI_p=V_sI_s$$ 4. **Solve the primary current.** $$I_p=(120)(0.50)/24=2.50\,\mathrm A$$ 5. **Check power.** $$P_{\mathrm{in}}=24(2.50)=60\,\mathrm W=P_{\mathrm{load}}$$ 6. **State the result.** $$2.5\,\mathrm A$$ **Result:** $2.5\,\mathrm A$

Worked application 11: An RL circuit with initial current · the current at the stated time

A series RL loop has resistance 6 Ω, inductance 3 H, and ideal source 12 V. Just before a switch establishes this loop, the inductor current is 0.3 A in the source-driven positive direction. The switch preserves a closed finite-resistance path. The calculation determines values at 0.3 s. Define inductor voltage as the passive drop along positive current. The calculation determines the current at the stated time. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Inductor current is continuous. Use the general exponential solution with the actual initial current, whether it is above or below the new steady value. 2. **Find the steady current and time constant.** $$I_\infty=V_s/R=2\,\mathrm A,\quad\tau=L/R=0.5\,\mathrm s$$ 3. **Use the arbitrary-initial-current solution.** $$I(t)=I_\infty+(I_0-I_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}=1.06702\,\mathrm A$$ 4. **Use the passive inductor-voltage convention.** $$V_L=L\,dI/dt=V_s-RI=5.59788\,\mathrm V$$ 5. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$I=2+(0.3-2)e^{-0.3/0.5}$$ 6. **Check the physical result.** The current lies between its initial value and the source-defined final value. 7. **State the result.** $$1.06702\,\mathrm A$$ **Result:** $1.06702\,\mathrm A$

Worked application 12: An RL circuit with initial current · the signed inductor voltage at that time

A series RL loop has resistance 6 Ω, inductance 3 H, and ideal source 12 V. Just before a switch establishes this loop, the inductor current is 0.3 A in the source-driven positive direction. The switch preserves a closed finite-resistance path. The calculation determines values at 0.3 s. Define inductor voltage as the passive drop along positive current. The calculation determines the signed inductor voltage at that time. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Inductor current is continuous. Use the general exponential solution with the actual initial current, whether it is above or below the new steady value. 2. **Find the steady current and time constant.** $$I_\infty=V_s/R=2\,\mathrm A,\quad\tau=L/R=0.5\,\mathrm s$$ 3. **Use the arbitrary-initial-current solution.** $$I(t)=I_\infty+(I_0-I_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}=1.06702\,\mathrm A$$ 4. **Use the passive inductor-voltage convention.** $$V_L=L\,dI/dt=V_s-RI=5.59788\,\mathrm V$$ 5. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$V_L=12-6(1.06702)=5.59788\,\mathrm V$$ 6. **Check the physical result.** The inductor voltage is negative while a current above the steady value decays. 7. **State the result.** $$5.59788\,\mathrm V$$ **Result:** $5.59788\,\mathrm V$

Worked application 13: An RL circuit with initial current · the stored magnetic energy

A series RL loop has resistance 6 Ω, inductance 3 H, and ideal source 12 V. Just before a switch establishes this loop, the inductor current is 0.3 A in the source-driven positive direction. sections.title: Wave quantities and wavelength conversion
sections.search:
## Light and optics: measure angles from the normal

Electromagnetic waves in vacuum satisfy $c = f\lambda$, with $c = 299{,}792{,}458\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$ exactly. Use $3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$ when the problem's precision supports that rounding. In a medium, $v = \frac{c}{n}$ and $v = f\lambda _{\mathrm{medium}}$. The frequency stays the same across a stationary interface; speed and wavelength can change.

Wave quantities and wavelength conversion

$$\lambda_0=c/f,\quad f=c/\lambda_0,\quad n=c/v,\quad \lambda_{medium}=\lambda_0/n.$$

**Worked example — primary p. 8.** With $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$, $4.0 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ corresponds to $750\,\mathrm{nm}$. A frequency of $7.9 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ corresponds to about $380\,\mathrm{nm}$. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength in the same medium. Convert $1\,\mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$ before calculating energy or speed.

The source introduces Newton's particle account, Huygens' wave account, and Young's interference evidence. Modern light has wave and particle behavior; neither everyday particles nor classical waves alone explain all observations. Ray optics approximates propagation by rays when wavelength is small compared with the relevant geometry.

sections.title: Photon energy and a necessary source correction
sections.search:
Photon energy and a necessary source correction

$$E_\gamma=hf=hc/\lambda_0,\quad K_{max}=hf-\phi,\quad f_0=\phi/h,\quad eV_{stop}=K_{max}.$$

The source introduces $E = hf$. The photoelectric relations above extend that idea to explain its experiment correctly. Photon energy must first supply work function $\phi$; excess energy becomes maximum electron kinetic energy. If $hf < \phi$, the model predicts no single-photon photoemission regardless of ordinary intensity increases.

Primary p. 10 incorrectly says electron kinetic energy is independent of frequency. Maximum kinetic energy INCREASES with frequency above threshold. At fixed frequency, higher intensity increases available photon rate, not each photon's energy. See the supplementary photoelectric reference in the source notes.

**Worked extension.** At $\lambda = 500\,\mathrm{nm}$, $E_{\gamma} = \frac{\left( 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \right) \left( 3.00 \times 10^{8} \right)}{\left( 500 \times 10^{-9} \right)} = 3.976 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J} \approx 2.482\,\mathrm{eV}$. For $\phi = 2.00\,\mathrm{eV}$, $K_{\mathrm{max}} \approx 0.482\,\mathrm{eV}$ and stopping-potential magnitude ≈ $0.482\,\mathrm{V}$. The boundary wavelength $\frac{hc}{\phi}$ is about $620\,\mathrm{nm}$. A longer wavelength cannot supply the required photon energy in this model.

sections.title: Reflection and surfaces
sections.search:
Reflection and surfaces

The law of reflection is $θ_{r} = θ_{i}$, with both angles measured from the surface NORMAL. A 30° angle to the surface is a 60° incidence angle. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in one plane. A smooth surface gives specular reflection; a rough surface gives diffuse reflection through differing local normals. Diffuse reflection does not mean each microscopic reflection violates the law.

**Derivation extension — stationary travel time.** For a reflection point sliding along a flat mirror in one uniform medium, total travel time is proportional to the sum of incoming and outgoing path lengths. Differentiate that sum with respect to the reflection point. Setting its derivative to zero gives equal sine ratios and hence $θ_{i} = θ_{r}$ in the ordinary reflection range.

Let the endpoints have horizontal separation d and heights $h_{1}$,$h_{2}$ above the mirror. Put the reflection point at horizontal coordinate x. The path length is $\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)} + \sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}$. Its derivative vanishes when $\frac{x}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)}} = \frac{\left( d - x \right)}{\sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}}$. These ratios are $\sin θ_{i}$ and $\sin θ_{r}$, measured from the vertical normal. Their equality gives the reflection law.

sections.title: Snell's law: derive it from phase matching
sections.search:
Snell's law: derive it from phase matching

At a stationary planar boundary, the wave phase must agree along the interface. Tangential wavevector components match: $k_{1} \sin \theta_{1} = k_{2} \sin \theta_{2}$. Since $k = \frac{2 \pi n}{\lambda_{0}}$ at a common frequency:

$$n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2,\quad \theta_2=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_1}{n_2}\sin\theta_1\right).$$

Rearrange to $n_{2} = \frac{n_{1} \sin \theta_{1}}{\sin \theta_{2}}$ or $\theta_{1} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{n_{2} \sin \theta_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)$ when the physical domain permits. The sine argument must lie between −1 and +1. In the ordinary incidence range, $n_{2} > n_{1}$ bends toward the normal; $n_{2} < n_{1}$ bends away. At normal incidence, direction stays normal although speed and wavelength can change.

**Independent derivation extension — stationary time.** With one endpoint above and the other below the interface, travel time is $t \left( x \right) = \left( \frac{n_{1}}{c} \right) \sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)} + \left( \frac{n_{2}}{c} \right) \sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}$. Differentiate with respect to x. Setting $\frac{dt}{dx} = 0$ gives $n_{1} \sin \theta_{1} - n_{2} \sin \theta_{2} = 0$. This reproduces Snell's law without assuming equal speeds in the two media. It applies to the stated uniform, stationary media and planar boundary.

**Worked example — primary p. 25.** Air $n_{1} = 1.00$ to water $n_{2} = 1.33$, $\theta_{1} = 45^{\circ}$. $\theta_{2} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{1.33} \right) \approx 32.12^{\circ}$. A value measured from the surface would be its complement.

sections.title: Several interfaces and the water–glass–air answer
sections.search:
Several interfaces and the water–glass–air answer

For parallel boundaries, the refracted angle inside the middle layer equals its incidence angle at the next boundary. Applying Snell twice gives $n_{1} \sin \theta_{1} = n_{2} \sin \theta_{2} = n_{3} \sin \theta_{3}$. The middle index cancels from the final angle relation, but not from the internal angle or lateral displacement.

**Worked correction — primary pp. 26–27.** Water $n = 1.3$, glass $n = 1.5$, air $n = 1.0$; start at 20° from the normal in water. Reflection in water gives $\theta_{A} = 20^{\circ}$. Glass refraction gives $\theta_{B} = \sin^{-1} \left[ \left( \frac{1.3}{1.5} \right) \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 17.24^{\circ}$. For parallel faces $\theta_{C} = 17.24^{\circ}$. Exit into air gives $\theta_{D} = \sin^{-1} \left[ 1.3 \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 26.40^{\circ}$, not the printed 20°. Returning to the original angle would require equal first and final indices, which this drawing does not have.

**Parallel-slab extension.** For slab thickness t, internal angle r, and external incidence i, perpendicular lateral displacement is $s = \frac{t \sin \left( i - r \right)}{\cos} r$. Derive it by drawing the internal path of length $\frac{t}{\cos} r$ and projecting its deviation from the original ray. This formula assumes parallel faces and an exit into the original medium without total internal reflection.

sections.title: Critical angle and total internal reflection
sections.search:
Critical angle and total internal reflection

Set the transmitted angle to 90° in Snell's law:

$$\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1,\quad \theta_c=\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1),\quad n_1>n_2.$$

Total internal reflection requires travel from larger n to smaller n AND $θ_{i} > θ_{c}$. At $θ_{i} = θ_{c}$, the ideal refracted ray grazes the boundary; it is the threshold, not a greater-angle case. If $n_{1} \le n_{2}$, there is no real critical angle for this direction of travel.

**Worked example.** Glass $n = 1.50$ to air $n = 1.00$ gives $θ_{c} \approx 41.81^{\circ}$. At 30°, refraction remains possible. At 50°, Snell's proposed transmitted sine exceeds one, so no propagating refracted ray exists in the elementary model. Use reflection rather than reporting a complex physical ray angle.

An optical fiber uses a higher-index core and lower-index cladding. Suitable core rays meet the boundary above its critical angle. The ideal ray picture guides them by total internal reflection. Real fibers still have attenuation, absorption, scattering, and bend losses; primary p. 31's “no absorption” wording is an idealization.

**Fiber acceptance extension.** In the meridional-ray model, let $n_{0}$ be the entrance-medium index, ncore the core index, and nclad the cladding index. For a ray inside the core at angle $\theta$ to its axis, wall incidence is $90^{\circ} - \theta$. At the limiting ray, $\cos \theta = \frac{n_{\mathrm{clad}}}{n_{\mathrm{core}}}$. Use $\sin^{2} \theta + \cos^{2} \theta = 1$, then apply Snell at the flat entrance:

$$n_0\sin\theta_{accept}=\sqrt{n_{core}^2-n_{clad}^2}=NA.$$

For a core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.46, $NA \approx 0.24249$. From air, the limiting entrance half-angle is about 14.03°. This is an angle to the fiber AXIS at the entrance, not the wall incidence angle. This ideal extension does not describe every skew ray, bend, or waveguide mode.

sections.title: Exam-scope note
sections.search:
Exam-scope note

The supplied Module 10 ends with reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection. It does not supply a complete thin-lens/mirror, diffraction, or polarization course. Extensions above are labeled. No finite set contains every possible derivation; these notes cover the supplied laws, standard inversions, limiting cases, and explicitly stated extensions. Always check the problem's geometry, physical assumptions, and available data before selecting an equation.

sections.title: Wavelengths, refractive index, and the source's physical models
sections.search:
Wavelengths, refractive index, and the source's physical models

**Source context — primary pp. 4–11.** All electromagnetic frequencies travel at c in vacuum. Visible light forms only a small part of the spectrum. Newton's historical particle description and Huygens' wave description precede modern wave–particle behavior. Young's interference experiment supports wave behavior. Einstein's photoelectric explanation connects photon energy to frequency.

**Ray approximation.** Rays describe propagation directions in geometric optics. In a uniform medium they travel along straight lines. In a medium with a varying refractive index, they can curve. The approximation works when the wavelength is small relative to the relevant geometric features. A ray is not a literal thin material strand.

:::example Visible-light frequency range to wavelength range
**Source:** Primary p. 8. **Given:** f ranges from $4.0 \times 10^{14}$ to $7.9 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Use $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$.

1. Start with $c = f\lambda$ and isolate $\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$.
2. Use the lowest frequency for the longest wavelength: $\lambda _{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{\left( 4.0 \times 10^{14} \right)} = 7.50 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$.
3. Convert meters to nanometers: $7.50 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{9} = 750\,\mathrm{nm}$.
4. Use the highest frequency for the shortest wavelength: $\lambda _{\mathrm{min}} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{\left( 7.9 \times 10^{14} \right)} \approx 3.79747 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m} = 379.747\,\mathrm{nm}$.
5. Report about 380–$750\,\mathrm{nm}$ in increasing wavelength order.

**Check.** Increasing frequency decreases wavelength. Reversing the endpoint order without stating the inverse relation makes the interval misleading.
:::

{{figure:m10-main:20|The primary refractive-index table. These are approximate material values; use the values given in a specific problem.}}

The table gives air 1.0003, ice 1.31, water 1.33, alcohol 1.36, fused quartz 1.46, crown glass 1.52, and diamond 2.42. Refractive index depends on material conditions and wavelength. The later water–glass–air exercise explicitly uses 1.3, 1.5, and 1.0 instead. Use those stated exercise values.

:::derivation Frequency stays fixed while speed and wavelength change
At a stationary interface, the oscillation rate must match on both sides. Otherwise, the boundary phase cannot remain matched over time. Thus $f_{1} = f_{2}$. Use $v = f\lambda$ and $n = \frac{c}{v}$:

$$\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}=\frac{v_2}{v_1}=\frac{n_1}{n_2},
\qquad \lambda_{medium}=\frac{\lambda_0}{n}.$$

For a labeled example, $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ vacuum light entering $n = 1.50$ glass has $v = 2.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$ and $\lambda _{\mathrm{glass}} = 400\,\mathrm{nm}$. Its frequency remains $5.00 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The shorter in-glass wavelength does not mean the photon acquires a higher frequency at this stationary boundary.
:::

sections.title: Photoelectric equations with the unit conversions shown
sections.search:
Photoelectric equations with the unit conversions shown

:::example Photon energy, kinetic energy, and stopping voltage
**Source starting point:** Primary p. 10 introduces $E_{\gamma} = hf$. The work-function and stopping-voltage calculations are labeled extensions.

**Given:** $\lambda_{0} = 500\,\mathrm{nm}$, $\phi = 2.00\,\mathrm{eV}$, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J} \cdot s$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$, and $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

1. Convert $\lambda_{0} = 500 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$.
2. Calculate $E_{\gamma} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{0}} = 3.9756 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.
3. Convert to electronvolts: $E_{\gamma} = \frac{3.9756}{1.602} = 2.48165\,\mathrm{eV}$.
4. Subtract the work function in the same unit: $K_{\mathrm{max}} = 2.48165 - 2.00 = 0.481648\,\mathrm{eV}$.
5. Divide Kmax in joules by e to obtain a stopping-potential magnitude of $0.481648\,\mathrm{V}$.
6. Use $\lambda thresh_{\mathrm{old}} = \frac{hc}{\phi} \approx 620.4\,\mathrm{nm}$ with these rounded constants.

**Check.** An energy of one electronvolt equals e times a potential difference of one volt. It is an energy unit, not a voltage unit. Here $\lambda_{0}$ is shorter than the threshold wavelength, so single-photon emission is energetically possible.
:::

:::derivation Threshold and stopping-potential rearrangements
Use conservation of energy for one emitted electron: $hf = \phi + K_{\mathrm{max}}$. At threshold, $K_{\mathrm{max}} = 0$, so $f_{0} = \frac{\phi}{h}$. With vacuum wavelength $\lambda_{0} = \frac{c}{f}$, the longest threshold wavelength is $\lambda thresh_{\mathrm{old}} = \frac{hc}{\phi}$.

For the stopping-potential magnitude, $eV_{\mathrm{stop}} = K_{\mathrm{max}}$. Therefore:

$$V_{stop}=\frac he f-\frac\phi e,
\qquad \phi=hf-eV_{stop}.$$

A Vstop-versus-frequency graph has slope $\frac{h}{e}$ and a zero-voltage intercept at $f_{0}$. At fixed frequency above threshold, ordinary intensity changes affect photon arrival rate rather than each photon's energy. Primary p. 10's frequency-independent kinetic-energy statement is incorrect.
:::

sections.title: Reflection and refraction: complete the source angle calculations
sections.search:
Reflection and refraction: complete the source angle calculations

**Reflection geometry.** Measure the incident and reflected angles from the same surface normal. If the incident ray is 30° above a flat surface, its incidence angle is 60°. Its reflected ray is also 60° from the normal, or 30° from the surface. Diffuse reflection comes from different microscopic normal directions on a rough surface; it does not replace the local reflection law.

:::derivation Reflection from a stationary-path calculation
Let the endpoints lie at heights $h_{1}$ and $h_{2}$ above a horizontal mirror, separated horizontally by d. Let the reflection point have horizontal coordinate x. In the same uniform medium, minimizing travel time also makes the optical path stationary.

$$L(x)=\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}+\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}.$$

1. Differentiate: $\frac{dL}{dx} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)}} - \frac{\left( d - x \right)}{\sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}}$.
2. Set $\frac{dL}{dx} = 0$.
3. Recognize the two ratios as $\sin θ_{i}$ and $\sin θ_{r}$, with angles from the normal.
4. Obtain $\sin θ_{i} = \sin θ_{r}$. For ordinary reflection angles between 0° and 90°, $θ_{i} = θ_{r}$.

This is a labeled derivation of the source's reflection law, not a new mirror-image equation.
:::

:::derivation Snell's law from stationary travel time
For endpoints in two uniform media separated by a flat interface, write:

$$t(x)=\frac{n_1}{c}\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}
+\frac{n_2}{c}\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}.$$

1. Differentiate with respect to the crossing position x.
2. Set $\frac{dt}{dx} = 0$ and multiply by c.
3. Replace the geometric ratios by the sines of the normal-based angles.

$$n_1\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}}
-n_2\frac{d-x}{\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}}=0
\Rightarrow n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2.$$

The same law follows from matching tangential wavevector components. Both derivations assume stationary media and a stationary planar interface. Different speeds require the n-weighted travel time; minimizing the unweighted geometric length would give the wrong refraction law.
:::

:::example Air into water at 45°
**Source:** Primary p. 25. Use $n_{1} = 1.00$ for air and $n_{2} = 1.33$ for water.

1. Write $1.00 \sin 45^{\circ} = 1.33 \sin \theta_{2}$.
2. Divide by 1.33: $\sin \theta_{2} = 0.531659$.
3. Use inverse sine in degree mode: $\theta_{2} \approx 32.1176^{\circ}$.
4. Report about 32.1° from the normal.

**Check.** The ray enters the higher-index medium and bends toward the normal, so its normal-based angle decreases. Do not multiply the angle 45° directly by an index ratio.
:::

{{figure:m10-main:26|The water–glass–air geometry. The two glass faces are parallel, but the first and final media have different indices.}}

:::example Water, glass, and air: calculate all four requested angles
**Sources:** Primary pp. 26–27. **Given:** Water $n = 1.3$, glass $n = 1.5$, air $n = 1.0$, and initial incidence 20° from the normal.

1. Reflection in water gives $\theta_{A} = 20^{\circ}$.
2. Apply Snell at the first boundary: $1.3 \sin 20^{\circ} = 1.5 \sin \theta_{B}$.
3. Calculate $\theta_{B} = \sin^{-1} \left[ \left( \frac{1.3}{1.5} \right) \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 17.2426^{\circ}$.
4. Use the parallel glass faces: $\theta_{C} = \theta_{B} \approx 17.2426^{\circ}$.
5. Apply Snell at the second boundary: $1.5 \sin \theta_{C} = 1.0 \sin \theta_{D}$.
6. Substitute the first-boundary relation to avoid early rounding: $\sin \theta_{D} = 1.3 \sin 20^{\circ}$.
7. Calculate $\theta_{D} \approx 26.3994^{\circ}$.

**Source correction.** The printed exit angle 20° is incorrect for the stated first and final indices. Parallel faces restore the original angle only when the first and final media have the same refractive index. Check each interface for total internal reflection before applying a transmitted-ray formula.
:::

sections.title: Total internal reflection, optical fibers, and useful inverse forms
sections.search:
Total internal reflection, optical fibers, and useful inverse forms

:::derivation Critical angle and the domain test
**Sources:** Primary pp. 22 and 28–31. At the threshold, the refracted angle is 90°. Insert it into Snell's law:

$$n_1\sin\theta_c=n_2\sin90^\circ=n_2
\Rightarrow\theta_c=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right).$$

1. Check $n_{1} > n_{2}$. Without a higher-to-lower index transition, there is no ordinary critical angle.
2. Calculate $θ_{c}$ from the normal.
3. Compare the actual incidence angle with $θ_{c}$.
4. Use refraction for $θ_{i} < θ_{c}$, a grazing transmitted ray at $θ_{i} = θ_{c}$, and total internal reflection for $θ_{i} > θ_{c}$.

If $\sin \theta_{2} = \left( \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} \right) \sin \theta_{1}$ exceeds one, no real propagating refracted ray satisfies this elementary model. Do not force the calculator to return a transmitted angle.
:::

:::example Glass–air and water–air thresholds
**Labeled numerical extensions of the source law.**

1. For $n_{1} = 1.50$ glass and $n_{2} = 1.00$ air, $θ_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1.50} \right) = 41.8103^{\circ}$.
2. At $θ_{i} = 30^{\circ}$, $\sin \theta_{2} = 1.50 \sin 30^{\circ} = 0.75$, so $\theta_{2} \approx 48.5904^{\circ}$.
3. At $θ_{i} = 50^{\circ}$, the proposed transmitted sine is $1.14907 > 1$. Total internal reflection occurs.
4. For water $n = 1.33$ to air, $θ_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1.33} \right) \approx 48.7535^{\circ}$.

**Check.** Reversing the direction to air → glass removes the total-internal-reflection condition. An “optically denser” medium means a larger refractive index here, not necessarily a larger mass density.
:::

**Fiber applications — primary pp. 30–31.** A higher-index core and lower-index cladding support total internal reflection for suitable rays. Fiber links carry information encoded in light. The source lists telephone and internet links, cable systems, medical imaging, and engineering inspection. Real fibers have losses from absorption, scattering, and bending. The cladding's role is optical confinement; it does not make every fiber perfectly lossless.

:::derivation Apparent depth at a flat surface: a labeled small-angle extension
Let an object lie a true depth h inside index $n_{1}$. An observer in index $n_{2}$ extends a refracted ray backward and sees apparent depth happ.

1. Draw a ray reaching the interface at horizontal offset x. Then $\tan \theta_{1} = \frac{x}{h}$ and $\tan \theta_{2} = x$/happ.
2. For small normal-based angles, use $\sin \theta \approx \tan \theta \approx \theta$ in radians.
3. Insert the geometric ratios into Snell's law: $\frac{n_{1} x}{h} \approx n_{2} x$/happ.
4. Cancel x and solve happ ≈ $h \left( \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)$.

For a $1.00\,\mathrm{m}$ deep object in water $n_{1} = 1.33$ viewed from air $n_{2} = 1.00$, happ ≈ $0.752\,\mathrm{m}$. The small-angle restriction matters. This extension does not replace exact ray tracing at a large viewing angle.
:::

sections.title: Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation
sections.search:
Worked applications: models, calculations, and interpretation These worked examples apply the module concepts. Each example states its conditions, explains the model, and shows the complete working.

Worked application 1: Constant frequency during refraction

Monochromatic light crosses a stationary boundary from air into ordinary transparent glass. The stationary-boundary model distinguishes unchanged frequency and photon energy from changed speed and wavelength. 1. **Use the wave relation.** $$v=f\lambda$$ 2. **Use the refractive-index definition.** $$v=c/n$$ 3. **Keep frequency fixed at the stationary boundary.** $$\lambda_2/\lambda_1=v_2/v_1=n_1/n_2$$ 4. **Check photon energy.** $$E_\gamma=hf$$ **Result:** Frequency and photon energy.

Worked application 2: The angle convention in Snell’s law

A ray in air makes an angle of 20° with a flat glass surface. The angle measured from the glass surface converts to the incident angle measured from the normal. 1. **Draw the normal.** Draw a line perpendicular to the interface. 2. **Convert the angle.** $$\theta_i=90^\circ-20^\circ=70^\circ$$ 3. **Use the normal-based law.** $$n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$$ 4. **Keep a consistent convention.** Measure reflected and transmitted angles from their interface normals too. **Result:** $70^\circ$

Worked application 3: At and above the critical angle

A ray travels from a higher-index medium into a lower-index medium. The critical-angle condition determines the refracted ray direction in the ideal ray model. 1. **Start from Snell’s law.** $$n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$$ 2. **Set the limiting transmitted angle.** $$\theta_t=90^\circ$$ 3. **Solve the critical angle.** $$\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1\quad(n_1>n_2)$$ 4. **Check the boundary case.** Above this incident angle, Snell’s law gives no propagating transmitted ray. **Result:** The refracted ray runs along the boundary at 90° to the normal.

Worked application 4: Parallel layers and a missing exit ray

Light crosses parallel transparent layers. You calculate the final angle using $n_i\sin\theta_i=n_f\sin\theta_f$ and obtain $\sin\theta_f>1$. The transmission condition explains a calculated final sine greater than one across parallel layers. 1. **Keep the parallel-boundary invariant.** $$n\sin\theta=\text{constant}$$ 2. **Check each interface.** A real transmitted angle requires the sine magnitude to be at most one. 3. **Test the high-to-low limit.** $$\theta_i>\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1)\ \Rightarrow\ \text{total internal reflection}$$ 4. **State the limitation.** The direct initial-to-final formula does not guarantee that an exit ray exists. **Result:** There is no transmitted exit ray through that limiting interface; check total internal reflection.

Worked application 5: Intensity below the photoelectric threshold

In the ordinary one-photon photoelectric model, monochromatic light has photon energy below a metal’s work function. Its intensity doubles while frequency stays fixed. The one-photon energy threshold explains the result of doubling intensity at fixed, below-threshold frequency. 1. **Calculate energy per photon.** $$E_\gamma=hf$$ 2. **Apply the threshold condition.** $$hf<\phi$$ 3. **Separate intensity and frequency.** At fixed frequency, increased intensity increases photon arrival rate. 4. **Apply the stated model.** The photons still lack the energy needed to release an electron. Multiphoton processes are outside this question. **Result:** No photoemission occurs in this model.

Worked application 6: Wavelength inside water

Light with vacuum wavelength 400 nm enters water with refractive index 4/3. The boundary is stationary. The calculation determines its wavelength in water. 1. **Keep the frequency fixed.** $$f=c/\lambda_0$$ 2. **Use phase speed in the medium.** $$v=c/n$$ 3. **Combine the relations.** $$\lambda=v/f=\lambda_0/n$$ 4. **Substitute.** $$\lambda=400/(4/3)=300\,\mathrm{nm}$$ 5. **Check energy.** The frequency and photon energy stay the same across this stationary boundary. 6. **State the result.** $$300\,\mathrm{nm}$$ **Result:** $300\,\mathrm{nm}$

Worked application 7: Refraction from a surface angle

A ray in air ($n=1.00$) strikes glass ($n=1.50$) at 30° to the surface. The calculation determines the transmitted angle to the normal. 1. **Convert the incident angle.** $$\theta_1=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ$$ 2. **Apply Snell’s law.** $$(1.00)\sin60^\circ=(1.50)\sin\theta_2$$ 3. **Solve the sine first.** $$\sin\theta_2=\sin60^\circ/1.50=0.577350$$ 4. **Take the inverse sine.** $$\theta_2=\sin^{-1}(0.577350)$$ 5. **Check the direction.** The transmitted angle is less than 60°, so the ray bends toward the normal in glass. 6. **State the result.** $$35.2644\,{}^\circ$$ **Result:** $35.2644\,{}^\circ$

Worked application 8: An exit ray through three media

A ray in water ($n=4/3$) crosses glass ($n=1.50$) and then air ($n=1.00$). Both boundaries are parallel. The water angle is 40° to the normal. The calculation determines the final air angle to the normal. Check that transmission is possible. 1. **Find the parallel-layer invariant.** $$n_w\sin\theta_w=\frac43\sin40^\circ=0.857050$$ 2. **Check the glass angle.** $$\sin\theta_g=0.857050/1.50=0.571367$$ 3. **Check the final interface.** $$\sin\theta_a=0.857050/1.00<1$$ 4. **Calculate the exit angle.** $$\theta_a=\sin^{-1}(0.857050)$$ 5. **Check total internal reflection.** The glass-to-air interface transmits here. A larger starting angle can prevent an exit ray. 6. **State the result.** $$58.987\,{}^\circ$$ **Result:** $58.987\,{}^\circ$

Worked application 9: Photoelectric stopping potential

Light of wavelength 350 nm strikes a metal with work function 2.20 eV. The calculation determines the stopping-potential magnitude in the ordinary one-photon model. Use $h=6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$. 1. **Convert wavelength.** $$\lambda=350\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm m$$ 2. **Calculate photon energy in electronvolts.** $$E_\gamma(\mathrm{eV})=\frac{hc}{\lambda e}=3.54521\,\mathrm{eV}$$ 3. **Check threshold and subtract the work function.** $$K_{\max}=3.54521-2.20=1.34521\,\mathrm{eV}>0$$ 4. **Use the stopping relation.** $$eV_{\mathrm{stop}}=K_{\max}$$ 5. **Check the units.** An electron kinetic energy of 1.34521 eV corresponds to a stopping-potential magnitude of 1.34521 V. 6. **State the result.** $$1.34521\,\mathrm V$$ **Result:** $1.34521\,\mathrm V$

Worked application 10: the critical angle from wave speed

Light travels at $2.00\times10^{8}$ m/s inside a transparent medium. It approaches a boundary with air ($n=1.00$) from inside. Use vacuum $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The calculation determines the critical angle to the normal. 1. **Infer the refractive index.** $$n_1=c/v=(3.00\times10^8)/(2.00\times10^8)=1.50$$ 2. **Check the high-to-low condition.** $$n_1=1.50>n_2=1.00$$ 3. **Use the critical-angle relation.** $$\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3$$ 4. **Calculate the normal angle.** $$\theta_c=\sin^{-1}(2/3)$$ 5. **Check the limiting ray.** At this angle, the transmitted ray is along the boundary. Larger incident angles give total internal reflection in the ideal ray model. 6. **State the result.** $$41.8103\,{}^\circ$$ **Result:** $41.8103\,{}^\circ$

Worked application 11: Critical angle and fiber acceptance · the core-to-cladding critical angle to the interface normal

An ideal straight step-index fiber has core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.44. Its flat entrance face is perpendicular to the fiber axis and lies in air of index 1.00. The lateral displacement is the perpendicular separation of the emerging ray from the undeflected incident line. The calculation determines the internal angle to the normal. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Refraction changes the internal path. Parallel faces restore the original external direction but can shift the ray sideways. 2. **Find the angle inside the slab.** $$\sin r=\sin i/n_g\ \Rightarrow\ r=22.4814{}^\circ$$ 3. **Use the internal path length.** $$\ell=d/\cos r$$ 4. **Resolve the ray offset geometrically.** $$\delta=\ell\sin(i-r)=d\sin(i-r)/\cos r$$ 5. **Use the material phase speed.** $$t=\ell/(c/n_g)=n_gd/(c\cos r)$$ 6. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$r=\sin^{-1}(\sin35^\circ/1.5)$$ 7. **Check the physical result.** The glass angle is below the air incidence angle. 8. **State the result.** $$22.4814\,{}^\circ$$ **Result:** $22.4814\,{}^\circ$

Worked application 41: Infer an unknown transparent medium · the unknown refractive index

Light crosses from air of index 1.00 into an unknown transparent medium. The measured incidence and refraction angles are 50° and 30°, both to the normal. The light frequency is $5\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For a later reverse-path critical-angle question, the ray starts inside that medium toward air. The calculation determines the unknown refractive index. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Infer index from the measured Snell ratio. A stationary boundary preserves frequency, allowing speed and wavelength to follow from the same index. 2. **Infer the unknown index.** $$n_2=n_1\sin i/\sin r=\sin50^\circ/\sin30^\circ=1.53209$$ 3. **Recover medium speed and wavelength.** $$v=c/n_2,\quad\lambda=v/f$$ 4. **Check the reverse high-to-low boundary.** $$n_2>1\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_c=\sin^{-1}(1/n_2)$$ 5. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$n_2=\sin50^\circ/\sin30^\circ=1.53209$$ 6. **Check the physical result.** The ray bends toward the normal, consistent with an index greater than air. 7. **State the result.** $$1.53209$$ **Result:** $1.53209$
